metadata.title: Cognitive Load During Problem Solving: Effects on Learning
metadata.abstract_summary: Conventional means-ends problem solving imposes a cognitive load that competes directly with schema acquisition, so practicing it teaches problem solving badly; a differently structured practice format that avoids that load (worked examples, goal-free problems) teaches the same content faster.

sections.heading: Claims
sections.text:
As the authors state it:

> Considerable evidence indicates that domain specific knowledge in the form of schemas is the primary factor distinguishing experts from novices in problem‐solving skill. Evidence that conventional problem‐solving activity is not effective in schema acquisition is also accumulating. It is suggested that a major reason for the ineffectiveness of problem solving as a learning device, is that the cognitive processes required by the two activities overlap insufficiently, and that conventional problem solving in the form of means‐ends analysis requires a relatively large amount of cognitive processing capacity which is consequently unavailable for schema acquisition. A computational model and experimental evidence provide support for this contention. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: A computational model of means-ends analysis's processing demands, plus a series of controlled experiments comparing conventional problem-solving practice against goal-free and worked-example formats on maze and algebra/physics-style tasks, measuring transfer and learning speed to a matched test set.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- The core effect (worked examples and goal-free problems outperform means-ends practice for novices) has been replicated extensively in the cognitive load literature that followed.
- Sweller's own experiments are small, lab-based, short-duration tasks - strong internal validity, limited direct evidence for long-horizon or real-classroom transfer.
- The theory was substantially refined after this paper (germane vs. extraneous vs. intrinsic load), a distinction this 1988 paper does not yet draw.
